subject: astronomy
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: Approximately how long is one synodic month?
questions.explain: The synodic month, the interval between successive identical phases such as new moon to new moon, is about 29.5 days.

questions.q: Approximately how long is one sidereal month?
questions.explain: The sidereal month, the time for the Moon to complete one orbit of the Earth relative to the fixed stars, is about 27.3 days.

questions.q: Why is the synodic month longer than the sidereal month?
options: The Earth has moved along its orbit around the Sun, so the Moon must travel further to return to the same phase
The Moon slows down as it orbits the Earth
The Moon's orbit is tilted relative to the ecliptic
The Earth spins more slowly during a full moon
questions.explain: Because the Earth advances around the Sun during the month, the Moon needs extra time beyond one full orbit to realign with the Sun and repeat a phase.

questions.q: Which phase immediately follows a new moon?
questions.explain: After the new moon the illuminated portion grows, giving a waxing crescent before the first quarter.

questions.q: During a full moon, how are the Sun, Earth and Moon arranged?
options: The Earth lies roughly between the Sun and the Moon
The Moon lies roughly between the Sun and the Earth
The Sun lies between the Earth and the Moon
All three are at right angles
questions.explain: At full moon the Earth is between the Sun and Moon, so the Moon's fully sunlit face is turned towards us.

questions.q: What does it mean when the Moon is described as 'waxing'?
options: The illuminated portion we see is increasing
The illuminated portion we see is decreasing
The Moon is closest to the Earth
The Moon is not visible at all
questions.explain: Waxing means the lit fraction of the Moon's disc is growing, from new moon towards full moon.

questions.q: At first quarter, what fraction of the Moon's visible disc appears illuminated?
questions.explain: Despite the name 'quarter', which refers to a quarter of the way through the cycle, half of the Moon's visible disc is lit at first quarter.

questions.q: You see a thin crescent Moon low in the eastern sky just before sunrise. Which phase is this most likely to be?
questions.explain: A waning crescent rises shortly before the Sun and so is seen in the eastern sky just before dawn.

questions.q: A solar eclipse can only occur at which lunar phase?
questions.explain: A solar eclipse needs the Moon between the Earth and Sun, which happens at new moon.

questions.q: A lunar eclipse can only occur at which lunar phase?
questions.explain: A lunar eclipse requires the Earth between the Sun and Moon, casting its shadow on the Moon, which happens at full moon.

questions.q: Why does an eclipse not occur at every new moon and every full moon?
options: The Moon's orbit is tilted by about 5° to the ecliptic, so the alignment is usually imperfect
The Moon is too small to cast any shadow
The Earth stops rotating during those phases
The Sun is too bright to be blocked
questions.explain: The roughly 5° inclination of the Moon's orbit means it usually passes above or below the exact Sun-Earth line, so eclipses occur only near the nodes.

questions.q: In the context of eclipses, what is the umbra?
questions.explain: The umbra is the darkest, inner cone of shadow where the light source is completely blocked.

questions.q: Why does an annular solar eclipse occur instead of a total one?
options: The Moon is near apogee, so its angular size is too small to fully cover the Sun's disc
The Earth is directly between the Sun and Moon
The Moon is exactly at a node of its orbit
The Sun is closer to the Earth than usual
questions.explain: When the Moon is near apogee it appears slightly smaller than the Sun, leaving a bright ring, or annulus, of Sun visible.

questions.q: Which feature of the Sun becomes visible during totality in a total solar eclipse?
questions.explain: With the Sun's bright photosphere hidden, its faint outer atmosphere, the corona, can be seen during totality.

questions.q: At which lunar phases do spring tides occur?
questions.explain: Spring tides, with the largest tidal range, occur when the Sun and Moon are aligned at new and full moon so their pulls combine.

questions.q: Neap tides, which have the smallest tidal range, occur when the Sun and Moon are positioned how relative to the Earth?
options: At right angles to each other
In a straight line on the same side
In a straight line on opposite sides
questions.explain: At first and third quarter the Sun and Moon pull at right angles, partly cancelling, giving the small tidal range of neap tides.

questions.q: Although the Sun is far more massive than the Moon, why does the Moon have the greater effect on the Earth's tides?
options: The Moon is much closer, and the tidal effect falls off very sharply with distance
The Moon is more massive than the Sun
The Moon reflects sunlight onto the oceans
The Sun has no gravitational pull on the Earth
questions.explain: Tidal forces depend strongly on distance, so the Moon's proximity outweighs the Sun's far greater mass.

questions.q: Roughly how much time passes between one high tide and the next high tide at a coastal location?
questions.explain: There are two high tides in a tidal day of about 24 hours 50 minutes, so successive high tides are roughly 12 hours 25 minutes apart.

questions.q: The Sun and the Moon both have an angular diameter of about 0.5° as seen from the Earth. This coincidence chiefly explains why:
options: Total solar eclipses are possible, as the Moon can almost exactly cover the Sun's disc
The Moon produces its own light
The Moon is physically the same size as the Sun
questions.explain: Because their angular sizes are nearly equal, the Moon's disc can just cover the Sun's, making total solar eclipses possible.

questions.q: Given that spring tides occur when the Sun, Earth and Moon are in a straight line, how many times does a set of spring tides occur during one synodic month?
questions.explain: Alignment happens at both new moon and full moon, so spring tides occur twice in each synodic month.

specSource: Pearson Edexcel GCSE Astronomy (1AS0) specification; The Earth-Moon-Sun System
